We use the same settings as before with a ViT-Tiny, though with 4 ×4 patches for TinyImageNet. In Table 4, we see that our initialization leads to improvements in test accuracy over 5% for Tiny ImageNet and CIFAR-100, but only 0.39% for the perhaps-easier SVHN dataset. 6. Why does this initialization work? We have shown that our mimetic initialization is quite ef- fective for enhancing visual recognition on small datasets. Here, we propose some additional explanations for why our method is effective. The ﬁrst section concerns the query and key weights, while the next two investigate the somewhat- more-mysterious negative diagonal of the value and projec- tion product. Near-identity attention maps. In Fig. 2 and Eq. 8, we see that our initialization, much like pretraining, makes the 6Mimetic Initialization of Self-Attention Layers Table 5.Other initializations T-Fixup ZerO LayerScale Original LayerScale Our Version Our Initialization 85.38 87.41 89.90 88.68 91.38 attention maps somewhat similar to identity matrices, par- ticularly in earlier layers. The resemblance of our attention maps using our initialization to those in pretrained models is notable in itself. He et al. (2023) notes that forcing at- tention maps to be the identity avoids rank collapse, which can otherwise prevent trainability. However, they note that exact-identity attention cannot pass gradients to the query and key parameters, meaning it is not actually a viable ini- tialization technique. We hypothesize that our initialization strikes a balance between untrained attention maps (as in Fig. 2a) and identity attention maps. LayerScale analogy In Touvron et al. (2021b), a simple technique called LayerScale is proposed to train deeper Transformers more effectively, in which the layer at a skip connection is multiplied by a learnable diagonal scaling matrix D: X′ l = Xl + D·SelfAttn(η(Xl)) (9) where ηdenotes LayerNorm. Here, we show that the way we initialize WV ,Wproj has a relatively weak resemblance to this technique. Considering Eq. 8, we approximate the attention maps after our initialization as being close to the identity, and assume that η(Xl) ≈Xl: X′ l = Xl + SelfAttn(η(Xl)) (10) ≈Xl + Iη(Xl)WV Wproj (11) ≈Xl + Iη(Xl)(αZ−βI) (due to our init) (12) ≈(I−β)Xl + αη(Xl)Z (13) Scaling Xl by (I −β) is similar in spirit to LayerScale, except in our case we are multiplying the left-hand instead of the right-hand term in the skip connection. This motivates us to compare our technique for setting to WV Wproj to using LayerScale, or our variant of LayerScale above. We searched ten choices of initialization for the diagonal elements in [0,1] for both LayerScale techniques, replacing our WV Wproj initialization, and report the best results in Table 5. Note we leave ourWQWT K initialization unchanged. Neither method achieves the performance of ours (with a difference of about 1.5%) though LayerScale comes closest. We conclude that the beneﬁts of our initialization extend beyond its possible similarity to LayerScale. Convolution analogy. Many works which successfuly train ViTs on small datasets do so by adding aspects of convolution, whether implicitly or explicitly. Here, we ex- plore adding locality to self-attention through convolutional biases: Softmax ( XWQWT KXT + γC ) , (14) where C is a doubly-block circulant convolution matrix and γ is a learnable scalar. Here, C is reminiscent of the PPT term in Eq. 8. This achieves 87.5% accuracy on CIFAR-10 within our usual training pipeline (without our init). For comparison, plain self-attention with no special initialization achieves 88.1% accuracy. Next, we move the convolution outside the softmax: Softmax ( XWQWT KXT ) + γC, (15) This has a more considerable advantange, resulting in 89.9% accuracy. Then, if we instead use C′ = Softmax(γC) to restrict C′to be all-positive, we achieve 75% accuracy. That is, it appears that the negative component of the convolution matrix is necessary. Thus, we hypothesize that initializing WV Wproj to have a negative diagonal is perhaps beneﬁcial for the same reason: this allows for some degree of “negative” or edge-detector- like spatial mixing to occur, a potentially useful starting point for the purpose of visual recognition. 7. Language Modeling While our method was primarily inspired by pretrained Vi- sion Transformers, in this section we investigate its potential for use in language models. As noted in Sec. 3 and seen in Fig. 9, we do not see precisely the same pattern in a pre- trained GPT-2 model as we do in a ViT. Nonetheless, we use the same technique here without modiﬁcation; we saw no improvement from, e.g., attempting to model the positive diagonals of WV Wproj. Small-scale Generally, it is hard to train Transformers from scratch on small language tasks (Dai et al., 2019); it requires substantial regularization, e.g., in the form of dropout. For word-level modeling on Penn TreeBank (PTB), we thus add one regularization tweak: word-level embed- ding dropout ( i.e., dropout of entire embedding vectors). This allows us to achieve sub-100 perplexity. We use a training setup identical to that of Bai et al. (2018), training for 100 epochs and reducing the learning rate when it plateaus. We used a vanilla Transformer with sinusoidal position embeddings, with embedding dimension 384, 12 layers, 8 attention heads, and weight-tied embeddings. First, on char-level PTB we did a small-scale hyperpa- rameter search for those αi,βi yielding the best validation BPC. We chose α1 = 0, β1 = 0.5, and α2 = β2 = 0.2. We 7Mimetic Initialization of Self-Attention Layers (a) WQWT K has a wider array of diagonal magnitudes (ﬁrst 3 heads shown). →Layers 1-12, ↓Attention Heads 1-3 of 12 (b) WV Wproj becomes positive in deeper layers. On char-level PTB, we see a small but signiﬁcant reduction in BPC from 1.233 to 1.210 through using our initialization. Similarly, we see a small reduction in perplexity on word-level PTB, from 84.84 to 82.34. (For both tasks, smaller is better.) While our initialization does not make a large amount of difference for these small-scale language tasks as it does for vision tasks, it does show a small amount of improvement. We suspect that it may be the case that a mimetic initializa- tion scheme more ﬁnely-tuned to the language setting may show still better performance. Medium-scale Next, we tried our initialization on a larger-scale task, WikiText-103. Here, we used an em- bedding dimension of 410 with 16 layers, 10 heads, and sinusoidal embeddings, with the same hyperparameters as for the previous task. As this dataset is around 110 times larger than PTB, we trained for only 50 epochs. Here, we see a more signiﬁcant performance gain from using our ini- tialization, reducing the test perplexity from 28.87 to 28.21 (see Table 6). While this is not a massive improvement, this is consistent with our observation on vision tasks that the improvement from our technique may be more signiﬁcant for larger models. Further, we also note that in this case the number of parameters being initialized is quite small relative to the total number of parameters of the language model due to the word embedding weights, something which does not occur with vision models. Conclusion Our proposed initialization technique for Transformers is particularly effective at improving performance on small- scale image recognition tasks, leading to an increase of over 5% accuracy in some cases. In other words, we address the problem that Vision Transformers are hard to train in ResNet-style pipelines solely through a structured initial- ization of the weights, without need for any kind of pre- training or architectural modiﬁcations. To a lesser extent, we demonstrated that our initialization leads to non-trivial gains on WikiText-103, showing that it also has potential to similarly improve language modeling on relatively small datasets. More broadly, we proposed a class of techniques we call mimetic initialization, in which we attempt to gain some beneﬁts of pretraining by mimicking the surface-level qualities of pretrained models. We speculate that it may be possible to use domain knowledge to “program” models before training in order to reach more desirable optima that may have been out of reach with a completely random ini- tialization. With better structured initialization techniques like our own, perhaps Transformers really are the universal architecture. 8Mimetic Initialization of Self-Attention Layers References Bai, S., Kolter, J. llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: The paper addresses the challenge of training vanilla Transformers on small datasets, where they typically underperform convolutional networks. It proposes a novel, learning-free, closed-form "mimetic initialization" scheme for self-attention layers that makes their weights resemble those of pre-trained Transformers. This initialization significantly improves training speed and final accuracies for vanilla Vision Transformers (ViTs) on vision tasks like CIFAR-10 (over 5% gain) and ImageNet (over 4% gain), and provides smaller gains for language modeling tasks like WikiText-103. The core idea is to initialize the product of query and key weights to approximate the identity (WQWT K "I") and the product of value and projection weights to approximate the negative identity (WV Wproj "-I"), which helps bridge the gap between ViTs and ResNet-style training pipelines without architectural modifications or pretraining.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: The proposed mimetic initialization is based on observations of pre-trained Transformer weights, specifically for vision models. It models the products of query/key (WQWT K) and value/projection (WV Wproj) matrices explicitly. For WQWT K, it approximates α1Z1 + β1I, and for WV Wproj, it approximates α2Z2 - β2I, where Zi are random normal matrices and αi, βi are parameters controlling the trade-off between noise and the diagonal. The actual WQ, WK, WV, Wproj matrices are then recovered using singular value decomposition (SVD). This method ensures that the query-key product has a positive diagonal and the value-projection product has a negative diagonal. The initialization is combined with standard sinusoidal position embeddings, as their interaction is crucial for performance.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: The initialization scheme was evaluated on various datasets and Transformer architectures. For **vision tasks**, experiments were conducted on CIFAR-10, ImageNet-1k, Tiny ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and SVHN, primarily using vanilla ViT-Tiny and ViT-Small models. Training pipelines included a ResNet-style (150 epochs) and a DeiT-style (300 epochs) approach. Augmentations used were RandAugment and Cutout, with a batch size of 512 or 1024, AdamW optimizer (3e-3 LR, 0.01 weight decay), and 100-300 epochs. Hyperparameters for αi, βi were tuned via a grid search on CIFAR-10. **Language modeling** experiments were performed on char-level Penn TreeBank (PTB), word-level PTB, and WikiText-103 using a vanilla Transformer with sinusoidal position embeddings (embedding dimension 384-410, 12-16 layers, 8-10 attention heads, weight-tied embeddings), 100 or 50 epochs, and word-level embedding dropout for PTB. Evaluation metrics included test accuracy for vision and BPC/perplexity for language modeling.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: The benefits of mimetic initialization in language modeling are smaller compared to vision tasks, suggesting that a scheme more finely tuned to language settings might be needed. The paper did not observe performance gains inversely proportional to the dataset size, which was a surprising finding regarding data efficiency, requiring more research to understand. The prominence of diagonals in weights tends to fade with depth, but mimicking this pattern did not yield improvements. While the initialization is comparable to or better than some architectural changes like GPSA, it's not universally superior to all such modifications in every configuration. The current study did not investigate the initialization of patch embedding and MLP layers.
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: The concept of "mimetic initialization" itself is proposed as worthy of future research, aiming to enhance the understanding of deep models' inner workings and lead to cheaper training and better optima. Specifically, tailoring mimetic initialization schemes more finely to language settings is suggested to potentially yield better performance. Further research on larger datasets is needed to fully understand how this initialization changes the data requirements of ViTs. The paper speculates that using domain knowledge to "program" models before training through structured initialization could lead to more desirable optima than random initialization.

new_method.method:
Open Problems: Even "small" language models (50-300 M parameters) still require >20 GB of GPU memory to train because memory scales with (1) three-or-more optimizer copies of the parameters and (2) the full activation stack for back-propagation. Existing techniques usually tackle ONE of these bottlenecks—e.g. reversible layers save activations, PEFT/LoRA saves parameter memory, in-place GELU or blockwise attention trims specific sub-modules—but no architecture jointly keeps BOTH parameter-state and activation memory below the capacity of a single consumer-grade 8-16 GB GPU while maintaining accuracy and speed. This prevents low-resource labs or on-device learning from pre-training or substantially fine-tuning language models.
Methods: We propose RASST (Reversible Adapter-Shared Structured Transformer), a unified architecture that collapses BOTH memory axes.
1.  Reversible skeleton: Each Transformer layer is a MEFT-style reversible block (F=attention, G=FFN) so activations are recomputed instead of stored.
2.  Shared Structured Base Weights:  For every linear map (Q,K,V,FFN), the large weight W is FACTORED as  W = U_s + Δ, where U_s is a frozen, 8-bit **structured unrestricted-rank matrix (SURM)** (circulant / Toeplitz) shared ACROSS ALL LAYERS; it provides high representational rank at negligible memory.
3.  Low-Rank Adapters with ReLoRA restarts: Δ = A·B^T (r≪d).  Only A,B are trainable.  Every R steps the low-rank update is merged into U_s (high-rank accumulation) and A,B are re-initialized, following ReLoRA to limit optimizer state.
4.  In-place Layers: Replace GELU and LayerNorm with ReGELU2 and Tempo Inplace-LN (needs only 2-8 bit masks) to avoid storing their inputs.
5.  Blockwise FlashAttention + chunked FFN as in BPT to keep per-layer workspace O(T) not O(T²).
6.  Optimizer: use K-FAC-reduce stored on CPU; only the small adapter parameters participate, so factors fit even on small GPUs.  For very tight budgets Adam8-bit can be swapped.
7.  Implementation detail: parameters stored in 8-bit, adapters in 16-bit; weight tying across even-odd layers is allowed and learned by a light RL agent (Dynamic Layer Tying) but costs no activations.
Experimental Setup: Pre-training:
• Models: GPT-Small (125 M), GPT-Medium (355 M) vanilla; RASST-125 M and RASST-355 M (same hidden sizes, r=32 adapters, shared SURM 8-bit).
• Hardware: single RTX-3080-Ti (12 GB) and single RTX-2060 (6 GB) to highlight low-memory regime.
• Data: WikiText-103 (pre-training) → fine-tune on PennTreeBank, GLUE.
• Metrics:   – Peak CUDA memory;   – Tokens/sec;   – Validation perplexity / GLUE score.
• Baselines:  (a) Vanilla model with gradient-checkpointing; (b) Reformer (rev only); (c) LoRA-128; (d) MEFT; (e) Tempo.
• Ablations: – remove reversible; – no in-place ops; – no structured base; – adapter rank 0 (shared weights only).
Robustness:
• Train with sequence length 1 K & 4 K to test BPT memory curve.
• Finetune with half-precision and full INT8 weight-only quantization.
Time-to-accuracy curves and wall-clock energy will be reported.
Result: Expected: 
• Peak training memory drops by 65-70 % vs vanilla and by 40 % vs best single-technique baseline, fitting 355 M model in 10 GB and 125 M in 5 GB.
• Throughput decreases <10 % compared to FlashAttention baseline; due to recomputation, wall-clock epoch time is similar.
• Validation PPL within +1 % of vanilla; GLUE average drops ≤0.5 points.
• Ablation confirms each component contributes (≈30 % memory from reversible, 20 % from in-place, 25 % from parameter scheme).
• Scaling to 4 K tokens shows linear memory growth, unlike vanilla.
• INT8 inference yields same accuracy → path to on-device.
Conclusion: RASST demonstrates that a carefully composed set of orthogonal ideas—reversible computation, structured shared weights and periodic low-rank updates, in-place activations, and blockwise kernels—enables full pre-training and fine-tuning of 100-300 M-parameter language models on commodity GPUs.  Academically, it unifies parameter- and activation-efficient lines of research and supplies the first empirical proof that sub-10 GB end-to-end training of non-toy LMs is feasible without severe accuracy loss.  Practically, this paves the way for personalized or domain-specific LMs trained at the edge, and for democratizing LM research in resource-constrained environments.  Future work: extend RASST to multimodal Transformers, explore learned SURM structures, and integrate online compression for the KV-cache during long-context inference.
